sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 49 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: But God will redeem my life from Sheol.
study.intro: Twenty verses form a wisdom poem addressed to the whole world: wealth cannot ransom a life from death, the rich leave everything behind, but God will redeem the faithful from Sheol.
study.context: The heading calls this a Psalm of the sons of Korah. Unlike most psalms it is not addressed to God; like Proverbs and Ecclesiastes it teaches. Verses 1–4 summon rich and poor to hear a 'riddle' set to the harp. Verses 5–12 argue that no wealth can ransom a life, ending with a refrain (verse 12) repeated with a change in verse 20. Verses 13–15 contrast the foolish, shepherded by Death into Sheol, with the speaker's confidence that God will redeem him from Sheol and 'take' him, the verb used of Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kings 2:3). Verses 16–20 counsel against envying the rich. Jesus' parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21) shares the theme. Sheol, the realm of the dead, is described in Old Testament terms; the notes do not read later doctrine into every phrase. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB, including the heading.
study.peopleNote: The sons of Korah are named in the heading. No other person is named. Planned paintings show treasure, tombs, sheep, lamps and landscapes; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Hear this, all you peoples
verses.heading: A wisdom summons to the world
verses.meaning: The heading names the sons of Korah. Instead of praying, the speaker addresses everyone on earth. 'All you peoples' and 'all inhabitants of the world' set a universal audience. The psalm is a teaching, like the wisdom of Proverbs. Its subject, death and wealth, concerns every human being. No nation or religion is exempt from the question it raises.
verses.context: Proverbs 8:4 has Wisdom calling, 'To you, O men, I call out,' and Ecclesiastes wrestles with death and wealth. Psalm 49 is one of the few psalms addressed to people rather than to God.
explore: All you peoples
The audience is the whole world. Its lesson concerns every human life.
Inhabitants of the world
The word suggests the passing world of time. Everyone listening lives in it briefly.
verses.reflect: Who would you want to hear the wisdom of this psalm? Why?
verses.alt: A herald's horn rests on a rock above a crossroads of many roads.

verses.title: Rich and poor alike
verses.heading: Wisdom for every class
verses.meaning: Both low and high, rich and poor alike. The audience is specified: people of every social level. The phrases pair opposites to include everyone. This matters for the psalm's theme. The rich may think wealth protects them; the poor may envy the rich. The coming lesson addresses both. Death will level all distinctions, and wisdom is offered equally.
verses.context: Proverbs 22:2 says, 'The rich and the poor have this in common: the LORD is Maker of them all,' and Job 3:19 says the small and great are there in death. Psalm 49:2 includes both.
explore: Low and high
Social rank does not matter here. All are addressed together.
Rich and poor
The lesson concerns wealth. Those who have much and those who have little both need it.
verses.reflect: How does your wealth or lack of it shape how you view others?
verses.alt: A gold coin and a clay cup sit side by side on a plain table.

verses.title: Wisdom and understanding
verses.heading: The speaker's meditation
verses.meaning: My mouth will impart wisdom, and the meditation of my heart will bring understanding. The speaker announces his purpose. He will speak wisdom that comes from careful thought. 'Meditation of my heart' suggests reflection over time. The teaching is not quick advice but considered insight. The verse invites the listener to slow down and think.
verses.context: Proverbs 4:5 urges, 'Get wisdom, get understanding,' and Psalm 19:14 prays that the meditation of my heart be pleasing to God. Psalm 49:3 combines both ideas.
explore: Impart wisdom
The speaker shares what he has learned. Wisdom is meant to be given.
Meditation of my heart
Understanding grows through reflection. It takes time and thought.
verses.reflect: What wisdom have you gained through careful reflection? Who could benefit from it?
verses.alt: A teacher's scroll and an hourglass rest in lamplight.

verses.title: A riddle with the harp
verses.heading: A proverb set to music
verses.meaning: I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will express my riddle with the harp. The speaker first listens, then speaks. He inclines his ear to a proverb, receiving wisdom before teaching it. Then he sets a riddle, a puzzling question, to the harp. Music carries the teaching. The riddle is the problem of death and wealth, which the psalm will unfold.
verses.context: Proverbs 1:6 speaks of understanding proverbs and riddles, and Psalm 78:2 says, 'I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter things hidden.' Psalm 49:4 sets such teaching to music.
explore: Incline my ear
The teacher listens first. Wisdom is received before it is shared.
My riddle
The puzzle is death and wealth. The psalm will explore it.
verses.reflect: What hard question about life do you wish someone would explain to you?
verses.alt: A harp rests beside a riddle carved into a clay tablet.

verses.title: Why should I fear?
verses.heading: Facing wealthy oppressors
verses.meaning: Why should I fear in times of trouble, when wicked usurpers surround me? The riddle is stated as a question. The speaker faces trouble from people who have cheated their way to power or who 'supplant' others. Literally the phrase may mean 'the iniquity of my heels,' perhaps those who trip him up. Why should he fear them? The rest of the psalm explains why not: their wealth cannot save them.
verses.context: Psalm 37:1 says, 'Do not fret because of evildoers,' and Psalm 73:3 confesses envy of the prosperous. Psalm 49:5 answers that fear by looking at death.
explore: Why should I fear?
The question states the riddle. The rest of the psalm answers why fear is unnecessary.
Wicked usurpers
The opponents are unjust and powerful. Their wealth gives them strength.
verses.reflect: Who makes you afraid because of their power? How might this psalm change that fear?
verses.alt: A modest cottage sits below a towering fortified mansion.

verses.title: Trust in wealth
verses.heading: The boast of the rich
verses.meaning: They trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches. The opponents are described. Their confidence rests in their money. They boast in it. The verse names a spiritual problem: trust placed in riches instead of God. The psalm will show that such trust fails at death. Jesus warns of this in the parable of the rich fool (Luke 12).
verses.context: Proverbs 11:28 says, 'He who trusts in his riches will fall,' and 1 Timothy 6:17 warns the rich not to set their hope on uncertain wealth. Psalm 49:6 describes such trust.
explore: Trust in their wealth
Money is their security. It takes the place of God.
Boast in riches
Their pride is in what they own. They glory in possessions rather than in God.
verses.reflect: What do you rely on for security? Is any of that trust misplaced?
verses.alt: A treasure room overflows with chests of gold and jewels.

verses.title: No ransom for a brother
verses.heading: Money cannot buy life
verses.meaning: No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. The heart of the riddle is given. No amount of money can redeem another person's life from death. Ransom was a payment to free someone. The psalm says no human can pay God for anyone's life, not even a brother's. The rich have no advantage here. The verse prepares for God's own redemption in verse 15.
verses.context: Exodus 21:30 allowed ransom payments for some legal cases, but Mark 10:45 says the Son of Man came to give His life as a ransom for many. Psalm 49:7 states that no human payment can buy life.
explore: Redeem his brother
No one can free another from death. Money cannot do it.
Pay his ransom
The price is beyond human means. Only God can redeem.
verses.reflect: What would it mean that no amount of money or effort can buy life?
verses.alt: Coins slide off an empty scale into the dust.

verses.title: Costly redemption
verses.heading: Payment never enough
verses.meaning: For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice. The price of a life is too high. Payment will never be enough. The verse is a parenthesis explaining verse 7. It does not mean life is worthless; it means life is so valuable that no human payment can match it. Only God can pay such a price.
verses.context: 1 Peter 1:18–19 says we were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, and Matthew 16:26 asks what a man can give in exchange for his soul.
explore: Costly
The price is very high. A human life is more precious than any sum.
Never can payment suffice
No human sum is enough. The cost of a life is beyond anyone's reach.
verses.reflect: How does knowing your life is precious to God affect how you see yourself?
verses.alt: A jeweler's scale balances gold against a single beating heart symbol of light.

verses.title: Not see decay
verses.heading: The dream of living forever
verses.meaning: That he should live on forever and not see decay. The sentence concludes. The rich may hope money can help them live forever and avoid the grave. But it cannot. 'Not see decay' means escaping death and the grave. Psalm 16:10 uses similar words, and the apostles applied that verse to Jesus' resurrection (Acts 2:27). Here the point is that no human can secure this by wealth.
verses.context: Psalm 16:10 says, 'You will not let Your Holy One see decay,' and Acts 2:27–31 applies it to Christ's resurrection. Psalm 49:9 says wealth cannot buy that outcome.
explore: Live on forever
The rich may want endless life. Money cannot provide it at any price.
Not see decay
Escaping the grave is beyond human power. Only God can do it.
verses.reflect: What do you hope for beyond death? Where does that hope rest?
verses.alt: An hourglass of gold sand runs out beside a crown.

verses.title: Wise and foolish both die
verses.heading: Leaving wealth to others
verses.meaning: For it is clear that wise men die, and the foolish and the senseless both perish and leave their wealth to others. Death comes to everyone. Even the wise die. The foolish also perish. All leave their wealth behind. The observation is plain and universal. Ecclesiastes 2:18–21 laments leaving wealth to someone who did not work for it. The verse invites humility about money.
verses.context: Ecclesiastes 2:16–18 notes that the wise die just like the fool, and Luke 12:20 asks who will get what the rich fool prepared. Psalm 49:10 states the same.
explore: Wise men die
Wisdom does not prevent death. The wise and the foolish die alike.
Leave their wealth
Riches stay behind. They pass to others who may never have earned them.
verses.reflect: What will you leave behind? How does that shape how you use what you have now?
verses.alt: Strangers carry off furniture from an empty mansion.

verses.title: Graves their eternal homes
verses.heading: Lands named after the dead
verses.meaning: Their graves are their eternal homes, their dwellings for endless generations, even though their lands were their namesakes. The rich named lands after themselves, hoping to be remembered. But their real dwelling is now the grave. Their 'eternal home' is a tomb. The irony is sharp. Their estates bear their names, but they live in a grave. Fame cannot outlast death.
verses.context: Genesis 4:17 records Cain naming a city after his son, and 2 Samuel 18:18 tells of Absalom setting up a pillar to keep his name. Psalm 49:11 shows such efforts end at the grave.
explore: Eternal homes
The grave is their final dwelling. Their mansions are left behind.
Lands their namesakes
The rich named lands after themselves. The names do not keep them alive.
verses.reflect: What are you trying to make your name known for? Will it matter in eternity?
verses.alt: Rock-cut tombs line a cliff above a valley of rich estates.

verses.title: Like the beasts
verses.heading: Wealth cannot endure
verses.meaning: But a man, despite his wealth, cannot endure; he is like the beasts that perish. This is the first refrain. However rich, a person does not remain. Literally, he does not 'spend the night' in his splendor. In death, he is like animals. The comparison is humbling. Humans are made in God's image, but in mortality they share the fate of animals. Wealth cannot change this.
verses.context: Psalm 49:20 repeats this refrain with an important change. Ecclesiastes 3:19 says the fate of man and beast is the same: as one dies, so dies the other.
explore: Cannot endure
Wealth gives no lasting security. Splendor passes overnight.
Like the beasts
In death, humans share the fate of animals. Mortality humbles all.
verses.reflect: How does remembering mortality change your view of wealth?
verses.alt: A gilded palace hall lies empty while wild goats wander through.

verses.title: The fate of the foolish
verses.heading: Those who follow foolish sayings
verses.meaning: This is the fate of the foolish and their followers who endorse their sayings. Selah. The psalm sums up. This end awaits not only foolish rich people but also those who admire them and repeat their sayings. Admirers of wealth share the danger of trusting it. Selah invites reflection before the next stanza. The verse warns against following the world's praise of riches.
verses.context: Proverbs 13:20 says, 'He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed.' Psalm 49:18 notes men praising the prosperous.
explore: Their followers
Admirers share the error. Praising wealth is dangerous.
Selah
The pause invites thought. The next stanza moves deeper.
verses.reflect: Whose sayings about wealth do you admire or repeat? Are they wise?
verses.alt: A crowd follows a gilded litter through a bazaar.

verses.title: Death their shepherd
verses.heading: Destined for Sheol
verses.meaning: Like sheep they are destined for Sheol. Death will be their shepherd. The upright will rule them in the morning, and their form will decay in Sheol, far from their lofty abode. The image is grim: the foolish rich are herded like sheep to the grave, and Death leads them. In contrast to Psalm 23, where the LORD is shepherd, here Death is the shepherd. 'In the morning' suggests a reversal when the upright prevail. Their bodies waste away far from their mansions.
verses.context: Psalm 23:1 says, 'The LORD is my shepherd,' and Isaiah 5:14 pictures Sheol opening its mouth. Psalm 49:14 shows Death shepherding the foolish.
explore: Death their shepherd
The image reverses Psalm 23. Death leads the foolish.
In the morning
The upright will prevail. A reversal is coming when the night of death ends.
verses.reflect: Who or what is leading your life? Where is it leading?
verses.alt: A flock of sheep files into a dark cave mouth at dusk.

verses.title: God will redeem my life
verses.heading: Taken to Himself
verses.meaning: But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself. Selah. This is the turning point and the answer to the riddle. No human can pay a ransom, but God will redeem. He will 'take' the speaker, the same verb used of Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kings 2:3). The verse expresses hope beyond death, at least of being kept by God from Sheol's grip. The notes present the hope without claiming the psalmist had a fully developed doctrine of resurrection.
verses.context: Genesis 5:24 says God took Enoch, and Psalm 73:24 says, 'Afterward You will receive me in glory.' Hosea 13:14 asks, 'Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol?' Psalm 49:15 rests on God doing what no one else can.
explore: But God
This is the turning point. God does what no human ransom could ever do.
Take me to Himself
The verb recalls Enoch and Elijah. God receives the faithful.
verses.reflect: How does this hope of being redeemed by God shape how you face death?
verses.alt: Dawn light breaks into a cave as a lamp is lit at its mouth.

verses.title: When a man grows rich
verses.heading: Do not fear the wealthy
verses.meaning: Do not be afraid when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases. The final stanza counsels the listener. Do not fear or envy the rich. Their houses may grow splendid, but that splendor is temporary. The question of verse 5, 'Why should I fear?', now has its answer. The rich are not truly powerful, because death strips them of everything.
verses.context: Psalm 37:7 says, 'Do not fret when men prosper in their ways,' and Proverbs 23:17 says, 'Do not let your heart envy sinners.' Psalm 49:16 answers verse 5.
explore: Do not be afraid
The counsel answers verse 5. The rich are not to be feared.
Splendor of his house
Wealth is visible and impressive. It will not last.
verses.reflect: Is there someone whose wealth or success makes you anxious or envious? How does this psalm help?
verses.alt: A mansion under construction rises higher with new marble columns.

verses.title: He will carry nothing away
verses.heading: Abundance left behind
verses.meaning: For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down. The reason not to fear is given. In death, the rich take nothing. Their abundance stays above ground. Job 1:21 says, 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return.' Paul echoes this in 1 Timothy 6:7. The verse is a sober reminder of what lasts.
verses.context: Job 1:21 and 1 Timothy 6:7 say we bring nothing into the world and can take nothing out. Ecclesiastes 5:15 says the same. Psalm 49:17 joins that wisdom.
explore: Carry nothing away
Death leaves wealth behind. Nothing goes with the dead.
Will not follow him
Abundance stays above ground. It cannot descend into the grave with its owner.
verses.reflect: What treasures are you storing up that will last beyond this life?
verses.alt: An open empty hand rests above a pile of coins.

verses.title: Men praise you when you prosper
verses.heading: Self-congratulation in life
verses.meaning: Though in his lifetime he blesses his soul, and men praise you when you prosper. The rich person congratulates himself during his life. Others praise him too, because people admire success. The verse shifts to 'you,' addressing the listener directly. Praise for prosperity is common, but it is not God's verdict. The next verse shows where such self-blessing ends.
verses.context: Luke 12:19 records the rich fool saying, 'Soul, you have many goods laid up,' and Hosea 12:8 says Ephraim boasts, 'I am very rich.' Psalm 49:18 describes such self-congratulation.
explore: Blesses his soul
He praises himself. He is satisfied with his wealth.
Men praise you
Society admires success. That praise is not lasting.
verses.reflect: Whose praise are you seeking? Is it the praise that lasts?
verses.alt: A banquet table overflows with food while guests raise cups.

verses.title: Never see the light
verses.heading: Joining the fathers
verses.meaning: He will join the generation of his fathers, who will never see the light of day. The self-congratulating rich man will die like his ancestors. He will join them in darkness. 'Never see the light' describes the grave as a place without light. This contrasts with verse 15, where God takes the faithful to Himself. The verse completes the contrast between the foolish rich and the redeemed.
verses.context: Job 10:21–22 describes the land of darkness and deep shadow, and Psalm 88:12 asks if God's wonders are known in the dark. Psalm 49:19 places the foolish rich there.
explore: Generation of his fathers
He joins his ancestors in death. Wealth makes no difference.
Light of day
The grave is pictured as dark. It contrasts with God's redemption.
verses.reflect: What hope do you hold that is brighter than the grave?
verses.alt: Ancient family tombs stand in a dark grove of cypress trees.

verses.title: Riches without understanding
verses.heading: The refrain with a change
verses.meaning: A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish. The refrain of verse 12 returns, but with a key change. Now it is not wealth itself that makes a person like the beasts, but wealth without understanding. Riches are not the problem; the problem is lacking wisdom to see that God alone redeems. The psalm ends by showing that understanding makes the difference.
verses.context: Psalm 49:12 says 'despite his wealth'; verse 20 adds 'without understanding.' Proverbs 3:13–14 says wisdom is better than silver. Psalm 49 ends by making understanding the key.
explore: Without understanding
Wealth without wisdom is dangerous. Understanding changes the outcome.
Like the beasts
Without wisdom, humans live and die like animals. With it, they trust God.
verses.reflect: What understanding do you need about your money and your life?
verses.alt: A wealthy man's ring lies abandoned in a meadow where cattle graze.
